Unraveling square and kagome lattice frustrated magnetism by scalable tensor networks

Xing-Yu Zhang Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, Ghent University, Krijgslaan 281, 9000 Gent, Belgium    Jutho Haegeman Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, Ghent University, Krijgslaan 281, 9000 Gent, Belgium    Yuchi He Email: yuchi.he@ugent.be Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, Ghent University, Krijgslaan 281, 9000 Gent, Belgium
November 6, 2026
Abstract

We extend the scalability of variational infinite two-dimensional tensor network methods with application to investigate frustrated magnetism of the square-lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model and kagome-lattice Heisenberg model. In the sign-problem-free limit of the square-lattice model, we achieve high ground-state energy precision comparable to quantum Monte Carlo methods. With no obstruction beyond this limit, our method obtains direct estimates of order parameters. For the square-lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model, we determine isotropic plaquette order in the valence-bond solid region. For the model near J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, and the kagome lattice Heisenberg model, our data indicate linear-dispersion gapless states. To probe the candidate spin-liquid nature of the highly frustrated cases, we go beyond inferring the absence of symmetry-breaking orders and analyze susceptibilities that characterize gapless spin liquids. By estimating scaling dimensions, our data indicate a stable gapless spin liquid on the kagome lattice, and competing scenarios for the intermediate regime of the square-lattice model. Our developments include parallelization and randomized low-rank methods and largely expand the frontier of high-precision variational numerics for quantum phases of matter.

I Introduction

Spin models on lattices provide good descriptions of quantum magnets with localized moments. A fascinating possibility is that frustration suppresses conventional symmetry-breaking orders and gives rise to emergent fermions and “light”, described by a U(1) gauge theory (quantum electrodynamics, QED) [1]. The emergent gauge group can also be ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} [2, 3], for example through Higgs condensation in a parent U(1) theory. Both belong to the broader landscape of quantum spin liquids [4]. Related deconfined gauge theories may also emerge only near a phase transition between two symmetry-breaking phases, as in deconfined quantum critical points (DQCPs) [5, 6, 7]. These emergent low-energy theories can produce characteristic signatures in observables such as thermal transport and neutron-scattering spectra, which have been actively searched for experimentally [8, 9, 10, 11, 12].

High-precision numerical solutions of spin-model ground states are essential for unraveling frustrated magnetism. They connect effective theories to experimental signatures in candidate systems and address the stability issue of emergent theories. Developing high-precision methods is therefore a central task in computational quantum many-body physics. While exact diagonalization (ED) is restricted to small clusters by the exponential growth of the Hilbert space, quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) can efficiently access low-temperature states as long as there is no sign problem. For the square-lattice Heisenberg model, for example, QMC can determine the ground-state energy with uncertainty at the 10−810^{-8} level [13]. Frustrating interactions, however, generally introduce a sign problem, as in the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model. QMC is also a major tool for lattice gauge theories, but simulations of compact QED3 with massless fermions remain challenging [14], leaving its infrared stability difficult to address. Variational methods offer an alternative by optimizing parametrized wavefunctions, with recent approaches employing increasingly expressive ansätze, notably tensor network states [15, 16] and, more recently, neural quantum states [17, 18, 19] and their combination [20]. Improved variational energies are generally expected to yield more accurate observables and correlations. These increasingly powerful methods are beginning to shed new light on prototypical models of frustrated quantum magnetism, racing to resolve questions that have been debated for decades.

One example is the square-lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model. A long-standing debate concerns whether an intermediate ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [21, 22, 23] exists between the Néel and valence-bond-solid (VBS) phases as J2J_{2} increases. Spectroscopic analyses of the termination of Néel order [24, 18, 25, 26] yield estimates of the critical J2J_{2} that shift substantially with increasing system size, potentially favoring a direct transition associated with a (proximate) DQCP [26]. Structure-factor and order-parameter analyses [27, 18, 28, 20] likewise give widely varying phase boundaries because of limited precision and strong finite-size effects. Even within the VBS regime, identifying the rotational symmetry pattern is difficult: structure-factor extrapolation diagnostics remain inconclusive [29], while pinned-order studies show spurious strong local anisotropy [27, 30].

Another example is the kagome Heisenberg model. Early numerical and theoretical studies established it as a leading candidate for a quantum-disordered ground state and a U(1) Dirac spin liquid [34]. The theory predicts coexisting characteristic susceptibilities, including dominant oscillatory valence-bond correlations and antiferromagnetic correlations [35, 36, 37, 38, 39]. A persistent numerical puzzle is that the predicted oscillatory valence-bond correlations are absent in several earlier [40, 41] and recent [42] variational studies. Twisted boundary conditions have been introduced to reveal this signature, but also produce less-expected chiral correlations [43]. This is consistent with the strong finite-size effects indicated by ED [44] and theoretical analysis [34]. More generally, identifying a gapless spin liquid requires approaching the low-energy limit and determining whether the predicted susceptibilities coexist, or whether one of the susceptibilities instead develops into an instability toward long-range order. Their scaling dimensions provide a quantitative diagnostic.

In this work, we substantially extend the scalability of two-dimensional tensor network methods [15, 16] and investigate the models above. Specifically, we use infinite projected entangled-pair states (iPEPS), which are formulated directly in the thermodynamic limit and thus give immediate access to order parameters. Their precision, however, is limited by how far the variational space, controlled by the bond dimension DD, can be scaled up in practice. We overcome long-standing computational bottlenecks with two developments: a near-ideal parallelization scheme for modern high-performance computing architectures, and a randomized low-rank method to treat longer-range couplings more efficiently.

These advances enable high-precision calculations. In the sign-problem-free limit of the square-lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model, we achieve precision comparable to QMC. Our results further reveal an isotropic plaquette order in the VBS regime, and we examine competing scenarios for the intermediate regime. For the kagome model, we find evidence for oscillatory valence-bond susceptibilities coexisting with other theoretically predicted susceptibilities, with extrapolations based on scaling-dimension analysis supporting a stable U(1) spin liquid.

II Results

We consider spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} models on square and kagome lattices with Heisenberg exchange interactions

H=J1​∑⟨i​j⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j,\displaystyle H=J_{1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}, (1)

where J1>0J_{1}>0 is the nearest-neighbor coupling, and the next-nearest-neighbor coupling J2>0J_{2}>0 is tuned for the square lattice model to enhance frustration.

For the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} square lattice model, our iPEPS determination of the order parameters is presented in Fig. 1a. The Néel antiferromagnetic order, schematically depicted in the upper-left inset, is the unfrustrated order at J2=0J_{2}=0. With increasing J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, the Néel order decreases. For J2/J1≥0.52J_{2}/J_{1}\geq 0.52, we find the emergence of plaquette valence-bond solid order, depicted in the right inset. Here, the nearest-neighbor bond energy E⟨i​j⟩=J1​⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩E_{\langle ij\rangle}=J_{1}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle spontaneously becomes nonuniform, with each of the four low-energy bonds forming a plaquette. The pattern preserves the C4​vC_{4v} rotational symmetry around the plaquette center.

The data are obtained using our variational iPEPS ansatz, dubbed the π\pi-mirror ansatz and illustrated in Fig. 2a. The wavefunction is represented by an infinite square lattice of site tensors connected through virtual bonds. Each tensor carries one physical leg of dimension d=2d=2 for the local spin-1/21/2 degree of freedom and four virtual legs of bond dimension DD, which controls the number of variational parameters. We use a 2×22\times 2 unit cell, allowing for plaquette-VBS order. For technical convenience, we perform the standard sublattice π\pi spin rotation, under which the Néel state can be represented by a single site-centered C4​vC_{4v}-symmetric tensor. Our ansatz contains only one independent tensor; the other three tensors in the unit cell are generated by mirror transformations and/or the π\pi spin rotation. We also impose time-reversal invariance by restricting the tensor entries to real values. Besides Néel order, this ansatz accommodates plaquette, columnar, and anisotropic plaquette VBS orders. For more efficient optimization at large DD, we further impose diagonal mirror symmetry on the independent tensor. High-precision calculations with a less-restricted ansatz show that the isotropic plaquette state is energetically favored (see Supplementary Information).

Physical observables in iPEPS can be evaluated and extrapolated with controlled precision by efficiently compressing the environment surrounding the region of interest. For example, the variational energy is obtained from expectation values ⟨ψ|𝐒i⋅𝐒j|ψ⟩/⟨ψ|ψ⟩\langle\psi|\mathbf{S}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_{j}|\psi\rangle/\langle\psi|\psi\rangle for nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor bonds. As illustrated in Fig. 2b, the corresponding bra-ket tensor network is contracted using environment tensors TT, which encode the effect of tensors outside the unit-cell region. A transfer matrix, illustrated in Fig. 2c, is constructed by contracting a strip of iPEPS tensors with the environment in one direction while leaving virtual indices open along the others. Correlation functions are then obtained by repeated application of the transfer matrix, and a correlation length ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi) follows from its leading eigenvalues. Ideally, ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi) approaches the true ground-state correlation length ξ\xi as D,χ→∞D,\chi\rightarrow\infty. In a VBS phase, where excitations are gapped, ξ\xi remains finite. In the Néel phase, spontaneous breaking of continuous SU(2) spin symmetry produces gapless spin-wave modes and a divergent correlation length. Likewise, gapped and gapless spin liquids are expected to exhibit finite and divergent correlation lengths, respectively. Nonetheless, at finite DD and environment bond dimension χ\chi, the transfer matrix has a finite effective spectrum and therefore imposes a finite correlation length ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi). For gapped phases, ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi) converges to the physical correlation length, as observed in our VBS data (see Supplementary Information). For gapless phases, by contrast, ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi) acts as a soft infrared cutoff that grows with increasing DD and χ\chi.

This gives rise to a procedure known as finite-correlation-length scaling [45, 46, 47], which we use to identify gapless phases and characterize their low-energy properties. The central idea is analogous to finite-size scaling, with the soft infrared cutoff ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi) replacing the finite system size LL. For gapless phases with linearly dispersing excitations, including the Néel phase and Dirac spin liquids, the finite-size correction to the energy density takes the form E⁡(L)=E∞+e1/L3+⋯E(L)=E_{\infty}+e_{1}/L^{3}+\cdots [13]. Correspondingly, for iPEPS we use E⁡(D,χ)=E∞+e1′/ξ​(D,χ)3+⋯E(D,\chi)=E_{\infty}+e^{\prime}_{1}/\xi(D,\chi)^{3}+\cdots [45, 47]. We next consider Néel order with the staggered magnetization 𝐦i=(−1)xi+yi​𝐒i\mathbf{m}_{i}=(-1)^{x_{i}+y_{i}}\mathbf{S}_{i}. In finite systems, where spontaneous symmetry breaking cannot be directly accessed, we use the normalized structure factor m2​(L)=N−2​∑i,j⟨𝐦i⋅𝐦j⟩m^{2}(L)=N^{-2}\sum_{i,j}\langle\mathbf{m}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{m}_{j}\rangle, with N=L2N=L^{2}, and extrapolate it as m2​(L)=m2+m1/L+⋯m^{2}(L)=m^{2}+m_{1}/L+\cdots. The leading correction follows from the long-distance magnon correlation ⟨𝐦i⋅𝐦j⟩=m2+a/|𝐫i−𝐫j|+⋯\langle\mathbf{m}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{m}_{j}\rangle=m^{2}+a/|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|+\cdots. In iPEPS, by contrast, spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs directly in the thermodynamic limit, allowing the order parameter to be read out as m⁡(D,χ)=Nuc−1​∑α=1Nuc|⟨𝐒α⟩D,χ|m(D,\chi)=N_{\rm uc}^{-1}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{N_{\rm uc}}|\langle\mathbf{S}_{\alpha}\rangle_{D,\chi}|, where NucN_{\rm uc} is the number of physical spin sites in the unit cell. We use this per-site amplitude for both lattices throughout the figures. For the collinear Néel pattern with equal and opposite sublattice moments, it equals |⟨𝐦i⟩||\langle\mathbf{m}_{i}\rangle| and 12​|⟨𝐒A⟩−⟨𝐒B⟩|\tfrac{1}{2}|\langle\mathbf{S}_{A}\rangle-\langle\mathbf{S}_{B}\rangle|. For kagome, the local moment directions can differ, and the average of their magnitudes is distinct from the magnitude of their vector sum. The corresponding finite-correlation-length scaling is m2​(D,χ)=m2+m1′/ξ⁡(D,χ)+⋯m^{2}(D,\chi)=m^{2}+m^{\prime}_{1}/\xi(D,\chi)+\cdots.

For J2=0J_{2}=0, a recent QMC study [13] provides an unprecedentedly precise benchmark. With our large-scale calculations, we obtain the ground-state energy at a comparable precision, reaching the 10−810^{-8} level. Further details of this benchmark are provided in Methods.

For J2≠0J_{2}\neq 0, we systematically improve the precision by increasing DD and χ\chi. Figure 1b shows linear extrapolations of m2m^{2} versus 1/ξ⁡(D,χ)1/\xi(D,\chi), which yield the Néel order parameter shown in Fig. 1a. When the extrapolation instead gives an unphysical negative value of m2m^{2}, it indicates the absence of Néel order; this occurs in our data for J2/J1≥0.49J_{2}/J_{1}\geq 0.49. At the extensively studied point J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, Fig. 1c shows the corresponding energy extrapolation. Its linear behavior over a broad range of 1/[ξ⁡(D,χ)]31/[\xi(D,\chi)]^{3} provides strong evidence for gapless excitations with linear dispersion. We also compare our results with a recent iPEPS study [31] and state-of-the-art variational calculations on finite systems [32, 17, 33, 19, 20]. Our best finite-DD results already lie remarkably close to the extrapolated energies, which enables a leading resolution of the low-energy physics. A more detailed evaluation shows that the difference is below 10−410^{-4} (see Methods).

By determining the order parameters, our data identify a region [shaded in Fig. 1a] absent of symmetry-breaking orders. Among the referenced literature, our estimate is close to the level-spectroscopy result of Ref. [18], with the region notably narrower on the VBS side than in the structure-factor analysis—based on the correlation ratio—of that same reference. This smaller J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} value for the VBS transition is also compatible with both earlier and more recent literature [24, 25, 26]. Determining the boundary of the Néel phase is subject to larger uncertainty, as reflected in the large extrapolation distance (small effective correlation length) of the Néel order in our calculation, Fig. 1b, as well as the large size-dependent shift of boundary estimation in previous level-spectroscopy studies [24, 18, 25, 26]. We believe that this reflects a general numerical challenge: the Néel order converges slowly as the low-energy limit is approached.

Beyond inferring the absence of order, unraveling spin liquids requires a direct probe of their defining characteristics. For the square-lattice model at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, our energy extrapolation analysis indicates linear gapless dispersion. This is consistent with a gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid as the leading candidate for the possible intermediate symmetric phase [23, 18]. Theoretically, its characteristics are coexisting Néel and VBS susceptibilities, manifesting as algebraic decay of two-point correlation functions of order parameters with characteristic exponents. Theoretical proposals for a gapless U(1) spin liquid exist for the kagome lattice owing to the lattice obstruction to the 2​π2\pi monopole instability present in the square lattice. The U(1) spin liquid is also characterized by coexisting Néel and VBS susceptibilities. Hence, before further investigation of the possible square-lattice spin liquid phase, we first present our data for the kagome model, and then comparatively investigate susceptibilities of both spin liquid candidates.

For the kagome lattice model, our data are based on optimizing a sublattice-merged iPEPS [49] (Fig. 3, upper-middle inset). We consider both a fully translation-invariant ansatz and a two-by-two enlarged unit cell. As expected, the 120°\degree AFM order (Fig. 3, upper-left inset) emerges in the fully translation-invariant ansatz, consistent with previous infinite tensor network studies [38, 48]. Finite-DD order that vanishes with increasing DD is an indication of corresponding susceptibilities. Our results for the two-by-two enlarged unit cell exhibit a much smaller magnetization and finite-DD valence-bond solid order (Fig. 3, lower-right inset). This is consistent with the oscillatory valence-bond susceptibilities predicted for U(1) spin liquids. Absence of evidence of the susceptibilities in previous numerical studies without twisted boundary conditions might be a finite-size effect. The VBS susceptibility is related to the gapless excitation at M points of the Brillouin zone found in tensor network studies [37, 48]. The energy extrapolation in 1/[ξ⁡(D,χ)]31/[\xi(D,\chi)]^{3} is shown in Fig. 3, consistent with gapless linear dispersion. Notably, the two different choices of unit cell yield nearly identical extrapolated results. We plot previous tensor network results for comparison.

We can now analyze the susceptibilities of the gapless spin liquid candidates, probing the characteristic signatures of the gapless phases. In Fig. 4, we plot m2m^{2} vs. 1/ξ1/\xi on a log-log scale for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} square lattice Heisenberg model with J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 and the kagome lattice Heisenberg model with 1×11\times 1 unit cell. Assuming gapless spin liquids, we thus use finite-correlation-length scaling [46, 47, 50], which requires the well-converged variational iPEPS data that we have access to. We fit

m2​(D,χ)∝[1/ξ⁡(D,χ)]2​Δm,\displaystyle m^{2}(D,\chi)\propto[1/\xi(D,\chi)]^{2\Delta_{m}}, (2)

where Δm\Delta_{m} is the dominant scaling dimension of the spin operator. The fits yield 2​Δm=1.020​(16)2\Delta_{m}=1.020(16) for the square lattice and 2​Δm=3.95​(11)2\Delta_{m}=3.95(11) for the kagome lattice. Using 2​Δm2\Delta_{m} as a proxy for the infrared scaling dimension of the spin–spin coupling term, the kagome value exceeds the space-time dimension d+1=3d+1=3, so this term is irrelevant, consistent with a stable gapless phase. On the square lattice, by contrast, 2​Δm<32\Delta_{m}<3, so the coupling is relevant and destabilizes the gapless state. For comparison, previous estimates for the square lattice, from fits to real-space correlation functions [18, 28] or from finite-size structure factors [20], all point to 2​Δm<1.52\Delta_{m}<1.5. Assuming an intermediate spin-liquid phase, we attribute these small values to the proximity of the Néel–spin-liquid critical point, or even the Néel phase itself, which may still dominate the correlations on the energy scales accessible to numerics. Effective field theory provides further insight. For both ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U(1) spin liquids, the bilinears of emergent fermions contribute to the spin-spin correlation functions. For gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin-liquid phases, scaling dimensions of bilinears are expected to follow those of free Dirac fermions, predicting ⟨𝐦i⋅𝐦j⟩=a/|𝐫i−𝐫j|4+⋯\langle\mathbf{m}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{m}_{j}\rangle=a/|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|^{4}+\cdots, namely 2​Δm=42\Delta_{m}=4. However, for a U(1) spin liquid, the bilinears may have different scaling dimensions, and there is also a possibly more dominant 4​π4\pi-flux monopole contribution [39]. Its scaling dimension ΔM\Delta_{M} is not precisely determined. The large-NfN_{f} expansions of compact QED3, uncontrolled at Nf=4N_{f}=4 flavors, yield 2​ΔM≈2.52\Delta_{M}\approx 2.5 [39], which is relevant and could destabilize QED3. Nevertheless, the proxy is close to the threshold 3. On the other hand, QMC [14] can only efficiently simulate the noncompact theory, giving 2​ΔM≈3.7​(3)2\Delta_{M}\approx 3.7(3) as another proxy. Since our fitting result for the dominant 2​Δm2\Delta_{m} of the kagome model is close to 4, it indicates that the monopole effects are either subdominant (irrelevant) or that the term has a small prefactor. In the Supplementary Information, we present our 2×22\times 2-unit-cell data for VBS susceptibilities.

In summary, by improving the scalability of the iPEPS method, we obtain high-precision data, which provide insights through extrapolation, including inferring the scaling dimension of susceptibilities. Our analysis indicates a possibly stable gapless spin liquid on the kagome lattice, and competing scenarios of the square lattice model near J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5. The gapless spin liquids are academically defined through the low-energy (infrared) limit. On the other hand, there are infrared cutoffs in the real world such as temperature and neutron scattering resolution. By approaching similar energy resolution, the iPEPS method can serve as a guide for spin liquid identification.

III Methods

We implement and develop numerical methods to evaluate and optimize two-dimensional tensor networks. The ingredients are the tensor network ansatz itself, the environment tensor determination, the evaluation of energies and other observables, the optimization, and the extrapolation of the results. As we show in Fig. 2b, observable evaluations use environments as input. Once the energy is evaluated, automatic differentiation (AD) [51] can generate energy gradients for energy-minimization optimization [52, 51, 53, 54], for which we use L-BFGS with a local preconditioner [55].

The iPEPS tensor fully encodes the variational wavefunction. The variational parameters correspond to the tensor entries, the number of which is proportional to d​D4dD^{4}. The variational manifold is enlarged with increasing DD and thereby enables better-optimized variational energies. The number of parameters of the environment tensors, proportional to χ2​D2\chi^{2}D^{2}, controls the precision of the energies, order parameters, and correlation lengths of an iPEPS. We label the calculated values with the corresponding DD and χ\chi. Exact evaluations of iPEPS expectation values are ideally obtained in the limit χev→∞\chi_{\mathrm{ev}}\rightarrow\infty, e.g., for the energy E⁡(D,χopt,χev=∞)E(D,\chi_{\mathrm{opt}},\chi_{\mathrm{ev}}=\infty). Note that here, we allow for using a different χopt\chi_{\mathrm{opt}} to compute the energy and its gradient during the optimization process, and could choose to only extrapolate to large χev\chi_{\mathrm{ev}} at convergence. A second extrapolation D,χopt→∞D,\chi_{\mathrm{opt}}\rightarrow\infty is needed. Here, we do not employ this approach, and rather use a one-shot extrapolation scheme [45] that takes data optimized and evaluated with the same χ\chi. No accompanying χev\chi_{\mathrm{ev}} extrapolation is needed. The example in Fig. 4 shows how these two schemes can induce different extrapolation results. For gapless phases, the one-shot extrapolation scheme assumes that the finite DD and χ\chi as a deviation from the exact limit can be unified to the soft IR cutoff ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi), provided we indeed use χopt=χev=χ\chi_{\mathrm{opt}}=\chi_{\mathrm{ev}}=\chi. More specifically, our data for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model indicate that E⁡(D,χ)E(D,\chi) is approaching the exact values monotonically from above in both χ\chi and DD, for sufficiently large χ\chi. This is indeed compatible with the extrapolation scheme and the observation that ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi) grows with DD and χ\chi. The monotonicity has been observed previously in studies based on C4​vC_{4v} iPEPS [51, 45] and iPEPS with mirror symmetry [56], which contains our π\pi-mirror ansatz. The mirror symmetry in these ansätze makes the norm converge monotonically from below in χ\chi [56], and is therefore likely relevant to the energy convergence behavior in χ\chi as well. Since finite-χ\chi evaluation practically induces energy overestimation for π\pi-mirror and C4​vC_{4v} iPEPS, we can get a better estimate of the energy for a given iPEPS by scaling up χ\chi. For example, for J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, the iPEPS has been optimized and evaluated at D=16,χ=1024D=16,\chi=1024; using χ=2048\chi=2048 for evaluation, we obtain E=−0.4967113E=-0.4967113, closer to the extrapolated result E=−0.4967446​(18)E=-0.4967446(18). Nonetheless, as mentioned above, the scheme we adopt uses data evaluated for the same value of χ\chi used during the optimization, but does allow us to collect data with different χopt=χev\chi_{\mathrm{opt}}=\chi_{\mathrm{ev}} for a given value of DD. The quality of the linear extrapolation of our J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} data (Fig. 1) demonstrates the self-consistency of this one-shot unified scheme. Note that the mirror symmetry is absent in our iPEPS ansatz for the kagome model, and it turns out that E⁡(D,χopt)E(D,\chi_{\mathrm{opt}}) may instead be smaller than E⁡(D,χopt,χev=∞)E(D,\chi_{\mathrm{opt}},\chi_{\mathrm{ev}}=\infty). Therefore, we use sufficiently large environment bond dimensions during optimization and employ the minimal canonical form [57, 58] to improve numerical conditioning, rendering χ\chi-deviation effects negligible. Only one χ\chi is used per DD in Fig. 3.

As another demonstration and benchmark, we present in Fig. 5 our C4​vC_{4v} iPEPS result for the Heisenberg model (J2=0J_{2}=0) in comparison with the recent high-precision QMC reference [13]. Similar to Fig. 1, we use the system width (LL) of the finite-size QMC results and the soft IR cutoff [ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi)] of our iPEPS calculations as length scales to organize the plots. Note that in Fig. 1, variational finite-size results from the literature were not extrapolated to L→∞L\rightarrow\infty because the variational errors were not guaranteed to be sufficiently small. In contrast, for the QMC results for the Heisenberg model, the sampled energies have error bars as small as 10−710^{-7}, and extrapolations with subleading corrections are performed in Ref. [13] and replicated in Fig. 5. In order to extrapolate our iPEPS results, we control their quality by insisting that the energy gradients for this model are as small as 10−610^{-6}. In the plot, we use blue and green to denote D=12D=12 and D=14D=14 data, optimized and evaluated with a series of χ\chi. The energies decrease monotonically with both DD and χ\chi. Note that we used even larger sets (and values) of DD and χ\chi for Fig. 1. The complete listing of the results per (D,χ)(D,\chi) pair can be found in the raw data set. The extrapolation only uses the leading term, i.e. 1/ξ​(D,χ)31/\xi(D,\chi)^{3} for energy and 1/ξ⁡(D,χ)1/\xi(D,\chi) for magnetization. The extrapolated energies agree with QMC up to 8 significant digits. Furthermore, our largest (D,χ)(D,\chi) result lies closer to the extrapolated energy than the result of the largest QMC system size. The precision is significantly improved compared to the previous implementation of the same extrapolation scheme [45]. This demonstrates the improved iPEPS data quality that is enabled by working with large DD and χ\chi.

However, this up-scaling of DD and χ\chi requires overcoming some key challenges, namely reducing the computational cost and being able to effectively utilize modern parallel computation architectures. These are known as bottlenecks of iPEPS methods. To achieve the latter, we introduce a scheme that realizes nearly ideal parallelization of the evaluation and optimization. To further help with the computational cost, we also propose a randomized loop contraction scheme for evaluating the next-nearest-neighbor coupling in the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model, which reduces complexity while maintaining sufficient precision.

We determine the environment tensor using variational uniform matrix product states (VUMPS) algorithms [59, 60, 61, 62]. Compared with the more conventional corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG) algorithm [63, 64], VUMPS does not require large-scale projector construction, and its computational cost is tensor-contraction dominated, with subleading costs associated with QR decompositions. The cost complexity of each iteration step is lower than for conventional CTMRG schemes, and scales as O⁡(D4​χ3)+O⁡(D6​χ2​d)O(D^{4}\chi^{3})+O(D^{6}\chi^{2}d) [62]. With the empirical choice χ=O⁡(D2)\chi=O(D^{2}), the cost scales as O⁡(D10)≈O⁡(N2.5)O(D^{10})\approx O(N^{2.5}), where NN is the number of variational parameters. Compared with CTMRG with revised projector solvers [65, 66, 67, 68], VUMPS can remain faster in practice 11 1 We limit our discussion to solving the conventional bilayer environment rather than the proxy layer-truncated environment, e.g., [69].

The principle behind the determination of the environment is to maximize the norm (per site) of iPEPS |⟨ψ|ψ⟩||\langle\psi|\psi\rangle|. In VUMPS, this amounts to sequentially finding the dominant eigenvector, for which the elementary step is to perform a linear map to an environment tensor. We first discuss the implementation of this step with a simple tensor parallelization scheme, which we dub 1DSlice. The linear map for the left environment (denoted as FLF_{L}) is illustrated in Fig. 6. Contracting FLF_{L} with the ket and bra iPEPS tensors and the top and bottom environment tensors gives the updated left environment tensor FL′F^{\prime}_{L}. The optimal order is denoted in Fig. 6. Note that the rank-four tensor FL′{F^{\prime}_{L}} can be obtained by computing the rank-three tensor slices FL,l=i′{F^{\prime}_{L,l=i}} for each i=1,..,χi=1,..,\chi independently. Computing these components one by one, instead of simultaneously, has the benefit of reducing the peak memory from O⁡(D4​χ2)O(D^{4}\chi^{2}) to O⁡(D2​χ2)O(D^{2}\chi^{2}). Such a common multi-tensor contraction trick has been known to the tensor network community [70]. We find that the independence of these tasks is naturally suitable for parallel computing, with a communication cost of O⁡(D2​χ2)O(D^{2}\chi^{2}) for the full process, since each computation device should have the full updated FLF_{L} in order to start the next iteration. Because the computational cost scales as O⁡(D4​χ3)+O⁡(D6​χ2​d)O(D^{4}\chi^{3})+O(D^{6}\chi^{2}d), the relative communication cost shrinks quickly when scaling up DD and χ\chi. Similar linear maps appear in other tensor network algorithms such as DMRG and CTMRG, for which tensor parallelization schemes exist for solving MPS (e.g., [71]) and 2D classical models [72]. What makes our scheme fairly simple and effective for iPEPS is the DD scaling specific to iPEPS, and VUMPS being dominated by the application of this linear map. In this 1DSlice scheme, memory is not distributed, in the sense that each computation device keeps the same data as single-device computation. In our implementation, this approach is sufficient for calculations reaching up to D=12D=12 using 64GB device memory. To scale up DD further and lift the bottleneck from single-device memory, we furthermore introduce a distributed memory scheme, which we dub 2DSlice (see Supplementary Information). These two schemes can be naturally extended to tensors with internal symmetries.

After determining the environments, the calculation of energies is performed term by term, each of which corresponds to a tensor contraction. With translation invariance, we sum over all couplings involving sites in one unit cell. For example, to compute the next-nearest neighbor (diagonal) coupling, we consider a cell of two-by-two bra-ket structure of iPEPS tensors contracted with surrounding environment tensors and with operators inserted in a diagonal pair of iPEPS physical legs, as was illustrated in Fig. 2b. Similarly, to compute the nearest-neighbor coupling, environments enclose two neighboring sites. The cost for computing the contraction for nearest-neighbor coupling scales as O⁡(D4​χ3)+O⁡(D6​χ2​d)O(D^{4}\chi^{3})+O(D^{6}\chi^{2}d), which is the same complexity as the VUMPS iteration. However, direct contraction for the next-nearest neighbor coupling incurs higher complexity O⁡(D6​χ3)O(D^{6}\chi^{3}). We introduce a randomized loop contraction scheme to reduce the cost to O⁡(D4​χ3)O(D^{4}\chi^{3}). This method finds a projector QQ, shown in Fig. 2d, to approximate the contraction while keeping high precision. For each corner of Fig. 2b, a bra-ket pair of iPEPS tensors contracts with two environment tensors, resulting in a corner tensor with dimension [D,D,χ,D,D,χ][D,D,\chi,D,D,\chi]. Grouping the legs, they can be viewed as a D2​χD^{2}\chi by D2​χD^{2}\chi matrix ℳ\mathcal{M} and ℳo\mathcal{M}_{o}, where oo represents the inserted operator. The evaluation of Fig. 2b can be regarded as a loop contraction Tr⁡(ℳ​ℳo​ℳ​ℳo)\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{M}\mathcal{M}_{o}\mathcal{M}\mathcal{M}_{o}). We replace this expression by Tr⁡(Q​Q†​ℳ​ℳo​ℳ​ℳo)\operatorname{Tr}(QQ^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}\mathcal{M}_{o}\mathcal{M}\mathcal{M}_{o}), where QQ is the isometric tensor in Fig. 2d, viewed as a D2​χD^{2}\chi by χ¯\bar{\chi} matrix. Here, χ¯\bar{\chi} is the control parameter that affects the accuracy of the approximation. Using the randomized QB method [73], QQ can be obtained from the QR decomposition ℳ​ℳo​ℳ​ℳo​Ω=Q​R\mathcal{M}\mathcal{M}_{o}\mathcal{M}\mathcal{M}_{o}\Omega=QR, where Ω\Omega is a D2​χD^{2}\chi by χ¯\bar{\chi} matrix with random Gaussian entries. For the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model, we find that χ¯=O⁡(χ)\bar{\chi}=O(\chi) is sufficient to maintain the precision 10−810^{-8}. The projector construction and its numerical validation are detailed in the Supplementary Information. This reveals a hidden approximate low-rank property, which may be general beyond this model.

Supplementary Information

1 Plaquette-order convergence at J2/J1=0.55J_{2}/J_{1}=0.55 for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} square lattice model

We provide data in Fig. 1 as evidence that the plaquette order parameter converges quickly with the PEPS bond dimension DD for J2/J1=0.55J_{2}/J_{1}=0.55. In the main text, we use the largest-DD data as a proxy for the plaquette order parameters in Fig. 1. This convergence analysis indicates that, at least away from the boundary (J2/J1=0.52J_{2}/J_{1}=0.52), the error of the proxy is sufficiently small.

We use the following ansatz to extrapolate the plaquette order parameter to D→∞D\rightarrow\infty:

OVBS​(D)=OVBS​(∞)+aDα.O_{\rm VBS}(D)=O_{\rm VBS}(\infty)+\frac{a}{D^{\alpha}}. (S1)

The three-parameter least-squares fit [Fig. 1a] using all five data points gives OVBS​(∞)=0.116O_{\rm VBS}(\infty)=0.116, and its difference from the D=16D=16 data is smaller than the marker size. To test this empirical extrapolation, we drop the two smallest-DD data points one by one in the fit, as a way to obtain an estimate of the extrapolation errors; the result changes by at most 3%3\%. Note that we only extrapolate in DD, as we assume that OVBS​(D,χ)O_{\rm VBS}(D,\chi) has already converged in χ\chi, with the value of χ\chi listed in the caption.

The VBS states are believed to be gapped with finite correlation length ξ\xi. This is unlike the magnetically ordered states where ξ\xi diverges as D,χ→∞D,\chi\rightarrow\infty. An extrapolation of ξ\xi is in general more complicated because ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi) is more χ\chi-sensitive than OVBS​(D,χ)O_{\rm VBS}(D,\chi). As a rough inference, we plot 1/ξ1/\xi vs. 1/D1/D in Fig. 1b, together with a tentative linear fit.

2 Evidence for plaquette VBS from a less-restricted π\pi-mirror ansatz

As introduced in the main text, our π\pi-mirror ansatz for the square lattice models implements two mirror symmetries in its trivial representation, thereby using one independent tensor to generate the 2×22\times 2 unit cell via horizontal and vertical flips. The ansatz is justified by its variational energy advantage. Plaquette, columnar, and anisotropic plaquette VBS orders are all compatible with this ansatz. Assuming a plaquette VBS order, we further implement the trivial representation of diagonal reflection symmetry to reduce the number of parameters and accelerate optimization. As a justification of this restriction and thus to determine whether the isotropic plaquette order is physically favored, we have also performed optimization without imposing this diagonal reflection restriction. The result (Fig. 2) for J2/J1=0.55J_{2}/J_{1}=0.55 provides confirmation for the rotationally symmetric plaquette VBS.

Our tensor plots in Fig. 2 of the main text have implied the trivial reflection symmetries by coloring. Here we give the formal definition by tensor-index permutation in Eq. S2 and Eq. S3. We order the tensor indices as (1,2,3,4,5)=(l,d,r,u,p)(1,2,3,4,5)=(l,d,r,u,p): left, down, right, and up virtual legs, followed by the physical leg. The diagram below uses the unit cell and tensor convention of main-text Fig. 2a, with PEPS tensors and bond energies labeled explicitly. The operator 𝒫σ{\cal P}_{\sigma} permutes the tensor indices into the listed order σ\sigma. We label the PEPS tensors as M~i​j\widetilde{M}_{ij}, where i=1,2i=1,2 runs from top to bottom and j=1,2j=1,2 from left to right in the 2×22\times 2 cell. This less-restricted ansatz uses

M~11=Mraw,M~12=𝒫(3,2,1,4,5)​Mraw,M~21=𝒫(1,4,3,2,5)​Mraw,M~22=𝒫(3,4,1,2,5)​Mraw,\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[width=89.6981pt]{figures/peps_index_convention.pdf}\end{gathered}\qquad\begin{aligned} \widetilde{M}_{11}&=M_{\rm raw},&\widetilde{M}_{12}&={\cal P}_{(3,2,1,4,5)}M_{\rm raw},\\ \widetilde{M}_{21}&={\cal P}_{(1,4,3,2,5)}M_{\rm raw},&\widetilde{M}_{22}&={\cal P}_{(3,4,1,2,5)}M_{\rm raw},\end{aligned} (S2)

The trivial diagonal reflection symmetry is a restriction on a single PEPS tensor

Mraw=𝒫(4,3,2,1,5)​Mraw.M_{\rm raw}={\cal P}_{(4,3,2,1,5)}M_{\rm raw}. (S3)

Without implementing Eq. S3, the horizontal and vertical strong-bond energies, EsHE_{s}^{H} and EsVE_{s}^{V}, are independent, and likewise for the weak-bond energies, EwHE_{w}^{H} and EwVE_{w}^{V}.

For J2/J1=0.55J_{2}/J_{1}=0.55 and working at D=10D=10, Fig. 2 shows that optimization at higher precision by using larger χ\chi points to a vanishing anisotropy, which is quantified as

δs=|EsH−EsV|,δw=|EwH−EwV|.\delta_{s}=\left|E_{s}^{H}-E_{s}^{V}\right|,\qquad\delta_{w}=\left|E_{w}^{H}-E_{w}^{V}\right|. (S4)

Increasing optimization χ\chi from 256 to 400, δs\delta_{s} decreases from 0.04090.0409 to 0.00260.0026 while δw\delta_{w} decreases from 0.03770.0377 to 0.00240.0024. We consider the small residual as a finite χ\chi and finite DD effect remaining.

Additional justification comes from the comparison with data with diagonal mirror symmetry restriction. For D=10,χ=400D=10,\chi=400, the optimized energy of unrestricted and restricted ansatz are −0.486225-0.486225 and −0.486213-0.486213 per site respectively. The energy difference (10−510^{-5}) is small compared to their difference to the ground state energy (>1×10−4>1\times 10^{-4}, bounded by our D=16D=16 result).

3 VBS susceptibilities from finite-correlation-length scaling

In the main text, we have performed finite-correlation-length scaling for the antiferromagnetic susceptibilities of the kagome Heisenberg model based on the 1×11\times 1 unit-cell data, shown in Fig. 4. As we show in the inset of Fig. 3 in the main text, the 2×22\times 2 unit-cell data have a dominant finite-DD VBS order. For a gapless spin liquid, this order is also supposed to scale to zero with increasing ξ⁡(D,χ)\xi(D,\chi). We characterize the finite-DD VBS order as Δ​Eb=max⁡(Eb)−min⁡(Eb)\Delta E_{b}=\max(E_{b})-\min(E_{b}), where the maximum and minimum are taken over all 24 bonds. We plot Δ​Eb\Delta E_{b} vs. 1/ξ1/\xi in Fig. 3. For a gapless spin liquid, we expect finite-correlation-length scaling Δ​Eb∝1/ξΔb\Delta E_{b}\propto 1/\xi^{\Delta_{b}}, where Δb>1.5\Delta_{b}>1.5 is again required in order for the VBS susceptibility to be stable against forming long-range order. The effective theory [41, 39] of the U(1) Dirac spin liquid predicts emergent symmetry leading to Δb=Δm\Delta_{b}=\Delta_{m}, where Δm\Delta_{m} is the spin scaling dimension of Eq. 2. The fit gives Δb=1.75​(25)\Delta_{b}=1.75(25), slightly below but consistent within the error bars with Δm=1.97​(6)\Delta_{m}=1.97(6) from the main text. Data at larger DD would sharpen this comparison and the margin above Δb=1.5\Delta_{b}=1.5.

4 Optimization and evaluation of iPEPS at different environment bond dimensions lead to deviations in extrapolations

We illustrate the distinction between increasing the environment dimension used to evaluate an iPEPS and reoptimizing its tensor at the larger dimension. Fig. 4 uses numerical data for a C4​vC_{4v} Heisenberg iPEPS with D=16D=16 as an illustrative example. A tensor optimized at χ=1024\chi=1024 is first evaluated at the same χ\chi, then reevaluated at χ=1536\chi=1536 without changing its entries. It is subsequently used to initialize optimization at χ=1536\chi=1536.

Increasing only the evaluation dimension lowers the energy by 3.43×10−7​J13.43\times 10^{-7}J_{1}, while ξ\xi grows from 15.742015.7420 to 16.117116.1171 (only 2.4%2.4\%, green arrow). Starting from this same tensor, just 50 L-BFGS optimization steps at χ=1536\chi=1536 lower the energy by a further 9.41×10−8​J19.41\times 10^{-8}J_{1}, but increase ξ\xi to 17.558317.5583 (8.9%8.9\%, red arrow). Thus, increasing χ\chi mainly improves the energy estimate in this example, whereas a short optimization continuation yields a much larger increase in correlation length despite its smaller energy gain. The D=12,14D=12,14 fit from main-text Fig. 5a is shown as an independent reference: both optimized points lie close to it, whereas the fixed-tensor reevaluation departs from it. The comparison illustrates why increasing χ\chi only during evaluation does not generally reproduce the sequence of tensors optimized and evaluated at the same χ\chi used in the one-shot scaling analysis.

5 Randomized loop contraction for evaluating diagonal J2J_{2} coupling

In Methods, we have introduced how to use a randomized low-rank method to reduce the computational complexity of computing the diagonal spin-exchange coupling J2​∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒jJ_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j} in the Hamiltonian of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} square lattice model. Here we provide more details of the method and the numerical evidence that the precision is maintained for practical purposes.

As a reiteration, the goal is to perform the contraction illustrated in Fig. 2b of the main text. The idea is to use a randomized low-rank method to find the projected basis QQ [Fig. 2d] that captures the approximate low-rank structure to reduce the cost of contraction. We replicate Fig. 2d from the main text to Fig. 5. After contracting the physical indices and grouping each corner with its adjacent boundary tensors, every corner becomes a matrix ℳ\mathcal{M} whose two fused indices have dimension D2​χD^{2}\chi. The operator-bearing corners are both denoted by ℳO^\mathcal{M}_{\hat{O}}. Cutting one bond of the resulting four-matrix loop defines an N×NN\times N effective transfer operator

KO^,O^=ℳO^​ℳ​ℳO^​ℳ,ZO^,O^=Tr⁡KO^,O^.K_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}=\mathcal{M}_{\hat{O}}\mathcal{M}\mathcal{M}_{\hat{O}}\mathcal{M},\qquad Z_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}=\operatorname{Tr}K_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}. (S5)

For next-nearest neighbor ⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle, the expectation value of the spin-exchange coupling on the variational state is calculated as

⟨ψ|𝐒i⋅𝐒j|ψ⟩⟨ψ|ψ⟩=ZS^x,S^x+ZS^y,S^y+ZS^z,S^zZI^,I^\frac{\langle\psi|\mathbf{S}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_{j}|\psi\rangle}{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle}=\frac{Z_{\hat{S}_{x},\hat{S}_{x}}+Z_{\hat{S}_{y},\hat{S}_{y}}+Z_{\hat{S}_{z},\hat{S}_{z}}}{Z_{\hat{I},\hat{I}}} (S6)

Forming KO^,O^K_{\hat{O},\hat{O}} has computational complexity O⁡(D6​χ3)O(D^{6}\chi^{3}), which is higher than the VUMPS iteration complexity.

We implement the randomized QB method [73] to approximately evaluate ZO^,O^Z_{\hat{O},\hat{O}} without forming KO^,O^K_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}. The randomized QB method is known to be able to recover exact low-rank structure and is good at revealing approximate low-rank structure. Let χ¯=χ+p\bar{\chi}=\chi+p and Ω∈ℂN×χ¯\Omega\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times\bar{\chi}} be a Gaussian random matrix. With the assumption that χ¯=χ\bar{\chi}=\chi may already be a good low-rank approximation for the projector to be constructed, the choice of p>0p>0 is dubbed oversampling. We calculate a matrix QO^,O^Q_{{}_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}} representing the projected basis satisfying QO^,O^†QO^,O^=IQ_{{}_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}}^{\dagger}Q_{{}_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}}=I, where II is the identity matrix. It can be obtained from

YO^,O^=KO^,O^​Ω,YO^,O^=QO^,O^​R,Y_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}=K_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}\Omega,\qquad Y_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}=Q_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}R, (S7)

where the second equation is a QR decomposition. With QQs, we can do the approximate loop contraction

ZO^,O^≈Tr⁡(QO^,O^†​KO^,O^​QO^,O^),Z_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}\approx\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(Q_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}^{\dagger}K_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}Q_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}\right), (S8)

as illustrated in Fig. 5. The above is a repetition of the minimal implementation of randomized loop contraction we introduce in Methods. In the randomized QB method, more subspace iterations qq to construct the YY matrix may help improve the contraction precision

YO^,O^(q)=(K​K†)q​K​ΩY^{(q)}_{\hat{O},\hat{O}}=(KK^{\dagger})^{q}K\Omega (S9)

Computing YY costs O⁡(D4​χ2​χ¯)O(D^{4}\chi^{2}\bar{\chi}), while the QR factorization costs O⁡(D2​χ​χ¯2)O(D^{2}\chi\bar{\chi}^{2}). Under the assumption that χ¯=O⁡(χ)\bar{\chi}=O(\chi) is sufficient to keep high precision, this cost amounts to

O⁡(D4​χ3),O(D^{4}\chi^{3}), (S10)

which is of the same order as the VUMPS iteration complexity.

Now we provide evidence that χ¯=O⁡(χ)\bar{\chi}=O(\chi) is sufficient in our calculation, and benchmark the choice of χ¯=χ+p\bar{\chi}=\chi+p and iteration qq. For relatively small DD, we can compute Eq. S6 without the randomized low-rank method. Thus, we can validate Eq. S8 against Eq. S5. As an example, we work with D=8D=8, J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5. For an optimized iPEPS and well-converged VUMPS environment (residuals below 10−1010^{-10}), we compute the diagonal coupling energies. The results for χ=128\chi=128 are summarized in Fig. 6. We use three random seeds to construct Ω\Omega. Fig. 6a indicates that the fluctuation of precision is small over random seeds. The errors here are around 10−710^{-7} and can be efficiently reduced by increasing pp. As a reference, we work with Float64 precision (10−1510^{-15}-10−1410^{-14}), and the VUMPS convergence residual is about 10−1010^{-10}. A precision of 10−710^{-7} is sufficient for our calculation of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model where our best ground-state energy precision is estimated as 10−510^{-5}. The results of Fig. 6 indicate that, in order to improve precision, using more iterations, i.e. q>0q>0, is less effective than oversampling pp. We also benchmark χ=256,512\chi=256,512 for D=8D=8. The calculation of q=0,p=0q=0,p=0 gives errors 1.48×10−81.48\times 10^{-8}, and 5.52×10−85.52\times 10^{-8} averaged over three fixed random seeds, compared to 1.73×10−71.73\times 10^{-7} for χ=128\chi=128.

We also benchmark randomized contraction in larger DD, for which direct contraction Eq. S5 is not available as a reference within currently reasonable computational resources. As an example, we contract the D=16D=16 state optimized with χ=1024\chi=1024. Direct contraction is not feasible at D=16D=16, so we use large oversampling pp extrapolation as the proxy E⁡(D=16,χ=1024,p=∞)=−0.496704261686E(D=16,\chi=1024,p=\infty)=-0.496704261686. The estimation errors and speed-up factor as a function of oversampling pp are shown in Fig. 7; the D=8D=8 data are replicated for comparison. We see that for the same ratio of p/χp/\chi, the errors in D=16D=16 are reduced.

6 Parallel algorithms for differentiable VUMPS

In Methods, we have explained a tensor contraction slicing scheme avoiding the naive intermediate large memory peak, which also naturally leads to a simple efficient parallelization scheme (1DSlice). The key idea is to divide the data of tensors by slicing one index with dimension χ\chi to several parts. Evaluating each part in series leads to reduction of peak memory. Evaluating parts in parallel gives the 1DSlice parallelization scheme. In this note, we first supplement the details of the technique to realize the O⁡(D2​χ2)O(D^{2}\chi^{2})-per-device memory cost (1DSlice) parallel optimization algorithm. We next explain our 2DSlice parallelization scheme, which extends the 1DSlice scheme and distributes the O⁡(D2​χ2)O(D^{2}\chi^{2}) memory to devices, lifting the limitation set by the single device memory. Finally, we show the profiling results for implementation of our methods on GPU devices across different computers. The results support that our parallelization scheme is near-ideal.

Slicing dominant environment tensor maps

Here, we extend the discussion of the slicing scheme introduced in Methods.

Most of the computational cost in the VUMPS fixed-point environment solve [59, 60] comes from repeated applications of the left, right, and center maps,

FL′\displaystyle F_{L}^{\prime} =ℱL​(FL,ALu,ALd,M),\displaystyle={\cal F}_{L}(F_{L},A_{L}^{u},A_{L}^{d},M),
FR′\displaystyle F_{R}^{\prime} =ℱR​(FR,ARu,ARd,M),\displaystyle={\cal F}_{R}(F_{R},A_{R}^{u},A_{R}^{d},M),
AC′\displaystyle A_{C}^{\prime} =ℱC​(AC,FL,FR,M).\displaystyle={\cal F}_{C}(A_{C},F_{L},F_{R},M). (S11)

Each of environment tensors (FLF_{L},FRF_{R},ALuA_{L}^{u},ALdA_{L}^{d}) has dimensions χ×D×D×χ\chi\times D\times D\times\chi, while the PEPS tensor MM has dimensions D×D×D×D×dD\times D\times D\times D\times d. In practice, χ=O⁡(D2)\chi=O(D^{2}), and dd is fixed by the Hamiltonian. These maps [Eq. (S11)] are contractions of input tensors. Except for the input data of tensors representing different environment tensors, all maps are identical. Thus we can focus on the first map, which we dub FLmap. The contraction is illustrated in Fig. 6 of the main text method section, with the same index labels as in Fig. 8, and can be written as

(FL′)r​g​h​l=∑i​j​e​k​p​f​a​b​c(FL)a​e​f​i​(ALd)i​j​k​l​Me​j​g​b​pu​Mf​k​h​c​pd​(ALu)a​b​c​r.(F_{L}^{\prime})_{rghl}=\sum_{ijekpfabc}(F_{L})_{aefi}(A_{L}^{d})_{ijkl}M^{u}_{ejgbp}M^{d}_{fkhcp}(A_{L}^{u})_{abcr}. (S12)

To perform the contraction with minimal computational cost, the order of summation (contraction) should follow the summation order in Eq. (S12), i.e., i​j​e​k​p​f​a​b​cijekpfabc from left to right, in other words, contracting the tensors one by one from left to right as mentioned in the caption of Fig. 6. The computational cost is

O⁡(χ3​D4)+O⁡(χ2​D6​d).\displaystyle O(\chi^{3}D^{4})+O(\chi^{2}D^{6}d). (S13)

The first intermediate, ∑i(FL)a​e​f​i​(ALd)i​j​k​l\sum_{i}(F_{L})_{aefi}(A_{L}^{d})_{ijkl}, carries indices a​e​f​j​k​laefjkl and contains χ2​D4\chi^{2}D^{4} entries. Further contraction with MuM^{u} yields a second intermediate with indices a​g​f​b​p​k​lagfbpkl and thus χ2​D4​d\chi^{2}D^{4}d entries. Because ll remains open throughout this procedure, each slice of ll of FL′F^{\prime}_{L} can be evaluated independently. We define the width ww as the number of consecutive ll components contracted together on one device. The intermediate storage of the contraction then gets reduced to

O⁡(w​χ​D4​d),\displaystyle O(w\chi D^{4}d), (S14)

compared with the naive O⁡(χ2​D4​d)O(\chi^{2}D^{4}d) peak. The case w=1w=1 evaluates one component of ll at a time; larger widths, such as w=4w=4 or 88, can improve GPU utilization.

For gradient evaluation, automatic differentiation needs the forward intermediates of Eq. S12. We recompute them one width-ww slice at a time and release them after applying its vector-Jacobian product (VJP). This preserves the reduced scaling of temporary memory given by Eq. S14.

Parallel computing on devices with separate memory (1DSlice)

As introduced in Methods, 1DSlice evaluates ll-index slices of FL′F^{\prime}_{L} in parallel on devices (GPUs) with separate memory. Let ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p} denote the slices of ll index assigned to MPI (Message Passing Interface, a standard message-passing system) rank pp, where pp is also a label of an individual GPU. Since GPUs are usually identical, ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p} is usually an equal partition across PP devices, or as equal as possible. The GPU pp computes (FL′)ℒp(F_{L}^{\prime})_{\mathcal{L}_{p}} slices of FL′F_{L}^{\prime}. As long as P≪χP\ll\chi, to avoid possibly large intermediate peak memory explained above, each GPU evaluates a width ww subslice of (FL′)ℒp(F_{L}^{\prime})_{\mathcal{L}_{p}} at a time. After this local computation, each GPU holds only its assigned part of FL′F^{\prime}_{L}. However, the complete updated environment on every GPU is needed for the next iteration; this is accomplished via a communication operation known as AllGather in MPI. The MPI collective communication operations we use are illustrated in Fig. 9a–c; each acts within a communicator, the group of ranks that take part in it [Fig. 9d].

We count the communication data sent per GPU during one tensor map. Let

SE=q​χ2​D2,SM=q​d​D4S_{E}=q\chi^{2}D^{2},\qquad S_{M}=qdD^{4} (S15)

be the sizes in bytes of one environment tensor and the site tensor MM, with qq bytes per scalar.

The AllGather at the end of an FLmap has the communication data volume

V1​Dfwd≃cAG,E​SE,V_{\rm 1D}^{\rm fwd}\simeq c_{\rm AG,E}S_{E}, (S16)

where cAG,Ec_{\rm AG,E} denotes the coefficient that depends on the implementation details of AllGather.

In the backward propagation of FLmap to compute the gradient, each GPU propagates the adjoints through its own part of forward FLmap. Adjoints are the derivatives of energy with respect to the corresponding tensors, denoted by bars. The local VJP is

(F¯L[p],A¯Lu,[p],A¯Ld,[p],M¯[p])=[D​ℱL​(FL,ALu,(ALd)ℒp,M)]∗​(FL′¯)ℒp.\left(\overline{F}_{L}^{[p]},\overline{A}_{L}^{u,[p]},\overline{A}_{L}^{d,[p]},\overline{M}^{[p]}\right)=\left[\mathrm{D}{\cal F}_{L}\!\left(F_{L},A_{L}^{u},(A_{L}^{d})_{\mathcal{L}_{p}},M\right)\right]^{*}(\overline{F_{L}^{\prime}})_{\mathcal{L}_{p}}.

The superscript [p][p] marks the local contribution before communication. Here D​ℱL\mathrm{D}{\cal F}_{L} is the Jacobian of the dependent variables, and its adjoint action propagates the output adjoint to the four inputs by the chain rule. To reduce peak memory, we also subslice ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p} and evaluate ww components at a time. The shared-input contributions are summed locally, while A¯Ld,[p]\overline{A}_{L}^{d,[p]} contains disjoint ll intervals. The complete input adjoints are

F¯L\displaystyle\overline{F}_{L} =AllReduce⁡(F¯L[p]),\displaystyle=\operatorname{AllReduce}(\overline{F}_{L}^{[p]}), A¯Lu\displaystyle\overline{A}_{L}^{u} =AllReduce⁡(A¯Lu,[p]),\displaystyle=\operatorname{AllReduce}(\overline{A}_{L}^{u,[p]}),
A¯Ld\displaystyle\overline{A}_{L}^{d} =AllGather⁡(A¯Ld,[p]),\displaystyle=\operatorname{AllGather}(\overline{A}_{L}^{d,[p]}), M¯\displaystyle\overline{M} =AllReduce⁡(M¯[p]).\displaystyle=\operatorname{AllReduce}(\overline{M}^{[p]}).

Here M¯[p]\overline{M}^{[p]} includes the contributions through both PEPS layers. Replicated copies represent one logical tensor, so each output interval contributes to the VJP only once. The communication volume is therefore

V1​DVJP≃(2​cAR,E+cAG,E)​SE+cAR,M​SM.V_{\rm 1D}^{\rm VJP}\simeq(2c_{\rm AR,E}+c_{\rm AG,E})S_{E}+c_{\rm AR,M}S_{M}. (S17)

The last term communicates only the PEPS tensor gradient. Its size ratio SM/SE=d​D2/χ2S_{M}/S_{E}=dD^{2}/\chi^{2} is at most 0.11%0.11\% for the benchmarks below, so it constitutes only a small contribution to the volume. For equal partitions with w≤χ/Pw\leq\chi/P, the per-GPU working memory in bytes is

Mem1​D=O⁡(SE+q​χ​w​D4​d).\mathrm{Mem}_{\rm 1D}=O\!\left(S_{E}+q\chi wD^{4}d\right). (S18)

The intermediate temporary memory depends on ww and is independent of PP. Each GPU has persistent memory of complete environment tensors.

Parallel computing with distributed memory (2DSlice)

As we discussed, the 1DSlice parallel scheme has small communication cost, and the number of devices (GPUs) PP can scale with χ\chi. Since every device in 1DSlice parallelization has a full copy of environment tensors with memory SE=O⁡(D2​χ2)S_{E}=O(D^{2}\chi^{2}) and other data with similar sizes, the memory is not distributed. To overcome the limitation that data may not fit in a single device’s memory, we design a distributed memory parallelization scheme. Two indices of each environment tensor are sliced in this scheme, thus dubbed 2DSlice. This scheme has even smaller communication data, decreasing with the number of devices as 1/P1/\sqrt{P}. The number of communication operations, related to latency time cost, is another important quantity for practically efficient parallelization. A design principle of 2DSlice is striking a balance between memory saving and the number of communication operations.

We arrange the devices (e.g., GPUs) as an N1×N2N_{1}\times N_{2} grid, P=N1​N2P=N_{1}N_{2}, as shown in Fig. 8b. Row index r1=0,1,…,N1−1r_{1}=0,1,\dots,N_{1}-1 and column index r2=0,1,…,N2−1r_{2}=0,1,\dots,N_{2}-1 are assigned to devices as well as blocks of environment tensors. The slicing indices of environment tensors are the two bonds with dimension χ\chi.

In 2DSlice, each device persistently stores its assigned blocks of the environment tensors. Each device never needs the full environment tensor in evaluating environment maps such as Eq. S12. Thus the communication data is reduced. Now we focus on FLmap. The distributed input and output tensors are

FL​[ar1,e,f,ir2],ALu​[ar1,b,c,rr2],ALd​[ir1,j,k,lr2],FL′​[rr1,g,h,lr2].\begin{gathered}F_{L}[a_{r_{1}},e,f,i_{r_{2}}],\qquad A_{L}^{u}[a_{r_{1}},b,c,r_{r_{2}}],\\ A_{L}^{d}[i_{r_{1}},j,k,l_{r_{2}}],\qquad F_{L}^{\prime}[r_{r_{1}},g,h,l_{r_{2}}].\end{gathered} (S19)

Similar to the single-device and 1DSlice parallel contraction, to reduce the naive intermediate large memory peak, each device divides its local lr2l_{r_{2}} range into small slices containing at most ww consecutive values. Let αr2\alpha_{r_{2}} be one such slice. Devices in column r2r_{2} compute different ar1a_{r_{1}} contributions for the same slice, while different columns process different ll blocks. The first contraction is

∑i(FL)a​e​f​i​(ALd)i​j​k​l|a∈ar1,l∈αr2.\left.\sum_{i}(F_{L})_{aefi}(A_{L}^{d})_{ijkl}\right|_{a\in a_{r_{1}},\,l\in\alpha_{r_{2}}}. (S20)

Rank (r1,r2)(r_{1},r_{2}) stores FL​[ar1,e,f,ir2]F_{L}[a_{r_{1}},e,f,i_{r_{2}}] and ALd​[ir1,j,k,lr2]A_{L}^{d}[i_{r_{1}},j,k,l_{r_{2}}], but needs the full range of ii for contraction. A row AllGather of FLF_{L} and a column AllGather of ALdA_{L}^{d} provide data for the full range [Fig. 9]. We call the resulting tensor blocks row or column gathered slices: full range of one index is gathered, while the other remains distributed. The row and column gathered slices contain SE/N1S_{E}/N_{1} and SE/N2S_{E}/N_{2} bytes, respectively, compared with persistent storage SE/PS_{E}/P per environment tensor.

For the last contraction with ALuA_{L}^{u} in the FLmap (Eq. S12), a row AllGather is first performed to provide full range of rr index for ALuA_{L}^{u}. Since the result contains contributions from all slices of the aa index, a column ReduceScatter is performed over slices of aa, yielding FL′​[rr1,g,h,l∈αr2]F_{L}^{\prime}[r_{r_{1}},g,h,l\in\alpha_{r_{2}}].

An alternative strategy exchanges blocks one at a time, as in Cannon’s parallel matrix multiplication, to avoid storing full gathered slices. In practice, we find that gathering the row and column slices at once can have much lower latency.

In our VUMPS implementation, we usually perform kk FLmap iterations at a time. After the first time of row- and column AllGather for distributed ALuA^{u}_{L} and ALdA^{d}_{L}, we can keep them in memory during the kk iterations. Taking into account the above communication processes, the size of communication data per FLmap iteration (forward part of AD calculations) is estimated as

V¯2​Dfwd\displaystyle\overline{V}_{\rm 2D}^{\rm fwd} ≃SE​[cAGrowN1+cRScolN2+1k​(c~AGrowN1+c~AGcolN2)].\displaystyle\simeq S_{E}\left[\frac{c_{\rm AG}^{\rm row}}{N_{1}}+\frac{c_{\rm RS}^{\rm col}}{N_{2}}+\frac{1}{k}\left(\frac{\widetilde{c}_{\rm AG}^{\rm row}}{N_{1}}+\frac{\widetilde{c}_{\rm AG}^{\rm col}}{N_{2}}\right)\right]. (S21)

Following the same VJP analysis as in Eq. S17, with fixed-input gathers and gradient reductions performed once per solve, the mean volume over kk map VJPs is

V¯2​DVJP\displaystyle\overline{V}_{\rm 2D}^{\rm VJP} ≃SE[cAGrow+cRSrowN1+cAGcolN2\displaystyle\simeq S_{E}\left[\frac{c_{\rm AG}^{\rm row}+c_{\rm RS}^{\rm row}}{N_{1}}+\frac{c_{\rm AG}^{\rm col}}{N_{2}}\right.
+1k(c~AGrow+c~RSrowN1+c~AGcol+c~RScolN2)]+cAR,MSM.\displaystyle\quad\left.{}+\frac{1}{k}\left(\frac{\widetilde{c}_{\rm AG}^{\rm row}+\widetilde{c}_{\rm RS}^{\rm row}}{N_{1}}+\frac{\widetilde{c}_{\rm AG}^{\rm col}+\widetilde{c}_{\rm RS}^{\rm col}}{N_{2}}\right)\right]+c_{\rm AR,M}S_{M}. (S22)

The tilded coefficients are evaluated for the once-per-solve messages and need not equal those for the per-map slice messages. If the fixed ALA_{L} gathered slices are retained from the forward solve, their tilded AllGather terms vanish. For a balanced grid and implementations with bounded volume coefficients, these environment terms scale as O⁡(SE/P)O(S_{E}/\sqrt{P}), compared with O⁡(SE)O(S_{E}) in 1DSlice. The remaining global AllReduce communicates only the gradient of MM. Relative to the gathered-slice scale, SM/(SE/P)=P​d​D2/χ2S_{M}/(S_{E}/\sqrt{P})=\sqrt{P}\,dD^{2}/\chi^{2}, below 0.44%0.44\% throughout the map benchmarks, including P=16P=16.

The row and column gathered slices are transient. For equal blocks with w≤χ/N2w\leq\chi/N_{2}, each local FLmap intermediate retains χ/N1\chi/N_{1} values of aa and at most ww values of ll. The per-GPU working-memory bound is

Mem2​D=O⁡(SEP+SEN1+SEN2+q​χ​w​D4​dN1).\mathrm{Mem}_{\rm 2D}=O\!\left(\frac{S_{E}}{P}+\frac{S_{E}}{N_{1}}+\frac{S_{E}}{N_{2}}+\frac{q\chi wD^{4}d}{N_{1}}\right). (S23)

For fixed ww, the intermediate term decreases as 1/N11/N_{1}. On a balanced grid, both this term and the gathered slices decrease as 1/P1/\sqrt{P}, while the persistent environment decreases as 1/P1/P. These estimates describe the dominant storage of a map and its VJP; replicated site tensors and other solver state must also be included in the full memory budget. The generic MPI path supports nondivisible χ\chi by quotient-and-remainder partitioning, provided every block is nonempty. The NCCL path used in the benchmarks requires equal blocks, χmodN1=χmodN2=0\chi\bmod N_{1}=\chi\bmod N_{2}=0.

Besides the dominant environment maps, VUMPS has a canonicalization step with subdominant computational cost O⁡(D2​χ3)O(D^{2}\chi^{3}) that relates ARA_{R}, ALA_{L}, and ACA_{C}. An algorithm with distributed memory is needed to keep the environment tensor storage distributed. Our implementation uses distributed tall-skinny QR (TSQR) decomposition [76]. Additional data communications are needed for the preparation for TSQR. A row AllGather first assembles a (χ​D2/N1)×χ(\chi D^{2}/N_{1})\times\chi input panel for local QR. A column AllGather then assembles the N1N_{1} local χ×χ\chi\times\chi triangular factors for a second QR; each rank retains the required isometry block. The initial panel contains SE/N1S_{E}/N_{1} data, while the stacked factors contain N1​q​χ2N_{1}q\chi^{2} bytes and contribute a separate communication volume cAGQR​N1​q​χ2c_{\rm AG}^{\rm QR}N_{1}q\chi^{2} per rank. The two stages require O⁡(χ3​D2/N1+N1​χ3)O(\chi^{3}D^{2}/N_{1}+N_{1}\chi^{3}) work per rank. The right-gauge LQ construction (TSLQ) follows the transposed procedure, with N2N_{2} replacing N1N_{1} and row and column collectives interchanged. Reverse differentiation recomputes these gathers, applies the corresponding ReduceScatters to panel and factor adjoints, and AllReduces the adjoint of the replicated gauge matrix CC. At fixed process grid, the QR/LQ work is subleading in DD, and factor communication and storage lack the D2D^{2} factor of the gathered slices. The input/output panels and QR workspace still contribute at the gathered-slice memory scale.

Overlapping communication and computation

The communication overhead of our parallel schemes can be reduced by making some communication happen simultaneously with the computation. Since we always divide the ll index into width-ww slices that are evaluated sequentially on each device, the gathering communications of the computed slices can overlap the computation of the next slices.

Parallel performance benchmark and validation

Here we benchmark the parallelization algorithms on GPU clusters with the CUDA libraries for numerical linear algebra and the MPI and NCCL libraries for communications. Specifically, we use MareNostrum 5 nodes of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, which have four NVIDIA H100 64-GB GPUs per node, NVLink all-to-all communication within a node, and relatively slower InfiniBand communication across nodes. We work with Float64 data and set the local Hilbert-space dimension d=2d=2 in the benchmark.

In Fig. 10, we show the strong-scaling performance with the number of GPUs for computing the dominant VUMPS environment tensor maps (forward pass) and the corresponding backward vector-Jacobian products (VJPs) used for gradient evaluation. The reported timings are the minimum over ten trials and are close to the average runtime observed in full optimization tasks. As discussed above, the environment tensor maps constitute the dominant computational cost for contracting the tensor network and evaluating observables, while the backward pass dominates gradient-based optimization. Let T⁡(P)T(P) denote the runtime for a given forward or backward calculation using PP GPUs. The strong-scaling results in Fig. 10 are presented in terms of the speedup T⁡(1)/T⁡(P)T(1)/T(P) [Fig. 10a]. We choose D=8,10,12D=8,10,12 and χ=512,1024\chi=512,1024 in the benchmark. The averaged speedup turns out to be very close to PP. In other words, the parallel efficiency T⁡(1)/[T⁡(P)​P]T(1)/[T(P)P] is close to 100%100\% [Fig. 10b].

The speedup depends on the choice of DD and χ\chi, and the variation is shown as a colored band around the curves. In general, the more computationally demanding case is that with larger χ\chi and DD, where the efficiency increases. This is consistent with the fact that the communication data grow much slower in χ\chi and DD than the computation cost. However, this alone cannot explain efficiencies exceeding 100%100\%, which is most notable for the memory-distributed 2DSlice scheme at larger DD and χ\chi. This is because reducing peak memory per GPU helps each GPU run closer to peak performance. (At D=12D=12, the single-GPU run has nearly reached its memory limitation.) In our test, we adjust ll-leg (sub) slicing width w∈{1,2,4,8,16}w\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} for each run and choose its fastest timing. For different ww, the timing can differ by as much as 10%10\%, affected by peak memory reduction, kernel efficiency, and/or communication overhead.

In the test platform, the cross-node communication (2525 GB/s card-card) is much slower than in-node NVLink (900 GB/s) communication, but it does not seem to be a bottleneck, as we see that the two-node run is nearly as efficient as the single-node run [Fig. 10]. For example, for D=12D=12 and χ=1024\chi=1024, the 8-GPU 1DSlice FLmap forward pass takes 436436 ms, while the communication data divided by the peak communication speed is on the order of 11\ ms for NVLink and 1010\ ms for internode communication. This echoes our design principle of 2DSlice, for which the number of communication operations is kept small. As a good side for practical implementations, the tensor parallelization for iPEPS-VUMPS is quite different from some other applications in the sense that super high-speed communication like NVLink is less demanded.

The benchmark in Fig. 10 times single applications of the environment tensor maps. To verify that their parallel efficiency also determines that of the complete calculation, we time complete contraction (dominant tensor maps and TSQR/TSLQ canonicalizations) and energy evaluation along with the full-process reverse-mode differentiation. The results are compared with those of FLmap and its VJP in Table 1. For 2DSlice, we use four GPUs as the reference because the energy-gradient evaluation at D=12D=12, χ=1024\chi=1024 does not fit on a single GPU. For both schemes, the overall efficiency closely follows that of the environment tensor maps; the parallel performance of the complete calculation is thus determined by that of the environment tensor maps. The small deviations come from the operations outside the environment maps, mainly the canonicalization, whose cost is subleading in DD as discussed above. The efficiency exceeding 100%100\% of the D=8D=8 energy-gradient evaluation is an effect of reduced peak memory due to memory distribution, same as our observation for FLmap efficiencies in Fig. 10.

Besides the profiling on up to 16 GPUs mentioned above, we also deploy the calculations on larger-scale parallelization on the H200 nodes of the Sofia cluster at the Flemish Supercomputer Center (VSC). We summarize the elapsed time record for a working example for the square lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model in Table 2.

Most calculations of this work can be completed within a few days on 16 GPUs. The tests on up to 128 GPUs verify that parallel execution remains feasible at larger scale, in preparation for more demanding applications.
